title: Effort begins to fill the void left by terminated US climate report
gist: After the Trump administration cut funding for the US Global Change Research Program and removed contributing authors, ending work on the next National Climate Assessment, the American Geophysical Union and American Meteorological Society launched a 'US Climate Collection' of independently peer-reviewed papers (the first, by 175 authors, published simultaneously in two journals) to informally replace the federally coordinated report, flagging the AI data center boom's reshaping of US electricity demand as a topic needing fresh analysis.

themes.theme: Termination of the federal climate assessment

insights.claim: The Trump administration eliminated funding for the US Global Change Research Program and removed hundreds of contributing authors, effectively shutting down work on the next US National Climate Assessment, and took past reports offline, forcing others to host copies to keep the information accessible.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Removal of a legally required federal climate assessment creates an information vacuum for infrastructure planners, insurers, and policymakers who previously relied on it as an authoritative reference, and signals continued federal retrenchment from climate science funding.
insights.locator: Last year, the Trump administration did what it could

insights.claim: The National Climate Assessment reports are legally required, despite the administration's move to defund and dismantle the process that produces them.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: A legal-mandate-versus-actual-execution gap creates potential litigation or future-administration reversal risk, relevant to tracking regulatory/legal challenges to the report's termination.
insights.locator: And this all comes despite the fact that these reports are legally required

insights.claim: The American Geophysical Union and American Meteorological Society launched the 'US Climate Collection,' inviting teams of researchers to publish peer-reviewed papers in scientific journals that will be added to a centralized resource for future report-writers, rather than coordinating one giant unified report like the US Global Change Research Program or IPCC model.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Represents a structural shift from centralized, federally coordinated climate assessment to a distributed, professional-society-led model, a new institutional pathway for climate science synthesis that could become a template if federal funding for such work remains cut.

insights.claim: The first paper in the collection, authored by 175 scientists (many of whom had been working on the now-defunct US report), was published simultaneously in two journals — one from AGU, one from AMS — and is intended as a roadmap to prioritize future contributions rather than a full assessment itself.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: 175 authors publishing a coordinated roadmap paper demonstrates significant researcher buy-in and continuity of expertise despite the federal program's defunding, suggesting the scientific community is self-organizing around the gap.
insights.locator: The first paper has now been added to that collection

insights.claim: Melisa Kenney, a lead author on the roadmap paper, described the effort as 'seeding and accelerating a distributed synthesis effort rather than launching a centrally managed research program,' intended to support a network of climate assessment efforts at state, local, sectoral, or other scales.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Clarifies the strategic intent behind the Collection: it is explicitly designed as a decentralized, non-federal alternative infrastructure for climate knowledge production, which could persist even if federal programs remain defunded long-term.
insights.quote: I see this roadmap as seeding and accelerating a distributed synthesis effort rather than launching a centrally managed research program

themes.theme: Priority topics identified in the roadmap

insights.claim: The roadmap paper calls out that while renewable energy continues to get cheaper and see more deployment, the AI data center boom has significantly reshaped expectations regarding US electricity demand, an area needing updated climate/energy assessment.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Direct confirmation from a scientific roadmap paper that the AI data center buildout is now a first-order factor reshaping US electricity demand forecasts, relevant to power-sector investment and grid-planning decisions tied to AI infrastructure growth.
insights.locator: And while renewable energy continues to get cheaper

insights.claim: The paper highlights that climate modeling has begun incorporating machine-learning-based simulations and techniques to generate finer spatial-resolution simulations as recent developments assessment reports should catch up to.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Signals growing adoption of ML-based climate simulation techniques as a frontier research area, relevant to companies building AI-for-climate-modeling tools.
insights.locator: Climate modeling has dabbled in machine-learning-based simulations

insights.claim: The paper suggests future assessments could expand beyond national borders, potentially evaluating impacts in Canada or how trade links the US to climate impacts elsewhere in the world, since the effort is not bound by the US-only scope of the former National Climate Assessment.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: A potential expansion of scope to cross-border and trade-linked climate impacts represents a methodological evolution beyond what federally mandated US-only assessments previously covered.
